opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few things going on. The first is just contamination in the broad sense. It's not always that the exact test questions leak into training data. It's that the internet is full of material that's *distributionally* very close to the benchmark: the same problem templates, the same styles of reasoning, solutions to near-duplicates. So a model can look like it's reasoning from first principles when really it's pattern-matching against something it has effectively seen before. You only find out when you perturb the problem slightly, like changing the numbers, reframing the setup, or adding an irrelevant detail, and performance drops off a cliff.

The second is that benchmarks are, by construction, narrow. Someone sat down and decided what a good measurement of "math ability" or "coding ability" looks like, and that's always a proxy. Once a field optimizes hard against a proxy, you get Goodhart's law. People tune data mixtures, prompting, even evaluation harnesses toward that specific format, and the number goes up faster than the underlying capability does.

Third, a lot of benchmarks saturate in a misleading way. Going from 85 to 92 percent might mean the model got better at the long tail of genuinely hard problems, or it might mean it got better at the particular quirks of that dataset, like label noise or answer formatting. The headline number doesn't tell you which.

And the thing I care most about is that real-world generalization is about robustness under distribution shift. Can the model handle a task phrased in a way no one anticipated, or chain together skills it learned separately, or recognize when it doesn't know something? Static benchmarks are pretty bad at capturing that. That's why I think you want a portfolio: fresh held-out evals that get refreshed regularly, adversarial and perturbed versions of existing tests, and, honestly, a lot of qualitative testing with people actually trying to use the model for hard, open-ended work. In the end, the most honest signal is often whether it's useful to experts on problems they genuinely care about, not whether it tops a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says training material can contain benchmark-like templates, reasoning styles, and near-duplicate solutions, letting the model pattern-match on material it has effectively seen before.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot. The simplest framing is that a benchmark is a proxy, and the moment you optimize hard against a proxy, it stops being a good proxy. So you can have a model that scores extremely well on, say, a math benchmark, and the question you have to ask is: did it get there by learning math, or did it get there by learning the benchmark?

There are a few ways the second thing happens. The most obvious is contamination, where some version of the test set, or something very close to it, leaks into pretraining. That's hard to fully rule out at internet scale, and even near-duplicates matter. But the subtler issue is that benchmarks have a distribution. They have a style, a format, a set of problem types, and models are very good at picking up on surface regularities. So you can get a model that's great at "problems that look like MATH problems" without it being great at the underlying reasoning, and you don't find that out until you shift the distribution slightly, change the phrasing, or ask it to do something adjacent that a human who actually understood the material would find trivial.

The other thing I'd say is that benchmark scores are an average, and averages hide a lot. A model can score 90% and be failing on exactly the cases that matter for real use. When we look at models internally, the number is sort of the starting point. The interesting part is looking at the failures, looking at held-out problems that were written after the model was trained, and seeing whether the capability transfers to things that nobody wrote a benchmark for. That's the real test of generalization: does it work when you leave the training distribution, not just when you're inside it.

r001.rationale: The response describes benchmark-specific optimization and learning benchmark style and problem types, as well as contamination from test items or near-duplicates, as ways a model can score well without learning the underlying capability.

astra-6.text:
I think a benchmark is always a narrow slice of what we actually care about. You can get very good at that slice without learning something that transfers broadly. If you repeatedly use the same benchmark to guide your research, you’re effectively optimizing against it—even if you never explicitly train on the test set.

And then there’s the gap between answering a well-specified question and doing something useful in the real world. In practice, the model might need to figure out what the user means, handle missing information, or recover when an approach fails. A high aggregate score can hide weaknesses in all of those things.

So I’d want to see whether the capability holds up when you change the wording, introduce an unfamiliar setting, or require several steps to work together. The benchmark score is evidence, but it’s not the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response says repeatedly using a benchmark to guide research can lead to optimizing against it, but does not identify overtraining on examples highly similar to benchmark items as the mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a benchmark is a pretty narrow slice of what we actually want a model to do. You can get very good at that slice through training choices, through tuning against the benchmark, or because similar problems show up in the training data. And the score alone doesn’t tell you which of those happened.

What I’m more interested in is whether the model can take the underlying idea and use it when you change the setup. If you phrase the question differently, introduce an unfamiliar constraint, or ask it to combine skills in a new way, does it still work? A model can look extremely strong on familiar problems and then be surprisingly brittle under those changes. So benchmarks are useful signals, but you need a broader set of evaluations to understand how well that capability transfers.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can score well because similar problems appear in its training data, clearly identifying exposure to benchmark-like examples as a mechanism for benchmark-specific performance.
